items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: CSR and financial performance — the evidence is mixed but tilts positive
items.claim: Friede, Busch and Bassen's 2015 meta-analysis aggregated over 2,000 studies on the link between ESG (environmental, social, governance) factors and corporate financial performance. What did it find?

options.text: ESG and financial performance are negatively related across the board
Around 90% of studies found a non-negative relationship; the majority showed positive correlation between ESG performance and financial performance, though magnitudes are modest
No study has examined this question
ESG is required to be at least cost-neutral by law

items.reveal:
Friede, Busch and Bassen (Journal of Sustainable Finance and Investment, 2015) reviewed 2,200 empirical studies dating back to the 1970s. About 90% reported non-negative ESG-CFP relationships; ~63% reported positive.

Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times Magazine essay ('The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits') argued the opposite. The empirical question turns out to be less stark than either side claims — the effect is usually positive but small, and depends on which ESG element and which industry.
items.why: Strategy debates about CSR are often conducted without reference to the evidence. The aggregate finding is messier than either 'CSR is profitable' or 'CSR is a cost' implies.

items.title: Share price and intrinsic value can diverge for years
items.claim: Robert Shiller's work (Nobel 2013) showed stock prices vary much more than fundamental dividends would justify. What's the implication for share price as a measure of company performance?

options.text: Share price always equals intrinsic value at all times
Share prices can diverge from intrinsic value for extended periods (excess volatility); managers focused on quarterly share prices may make worse long-term decisions
Share price has no link to fundamentals ever
Only private firms have intrinsic value

items.reveal_title: Markets price emotions as well as cash flows
items.reveal:
Shiller's 1981 American Economic Review paper showed S&P 500 prices fluctuated 5-13x more than dividend-based fair value would justify. Tech bubble peaks (2000, 2021) and crisis troughs (2009, 2020) bookend this excess volatility.

Warren Buffett quotes Benjamin Graham: 'In the short run the market is a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine.' Managers paid largely in stock options can be incentivised to manage the voting machine rather than build long-term weight.
items.why: Headline share price moves often reflect investor sentiment as much as company performance. Compensation and strategy that anchor on share price import this volatility.
